doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Buckshot Marching Kazoo Orchestra at Hamilton
summary: He played trumpet with Hamilton's kazoo band while on a Countsmen college tour, after recalling Columbia band antics.

bands.name: Aaron Burr Lucky Shot Marching and Kazoo Orchestra

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Tell me about the Buckshot Marching Kazoo Orchestra.

Oh well yeah, this is my connection to Hamilton. When I was — first launched the Countsmen, the Basie alumni band, I briefly — we had a good first year. If I thought that that was going to be the best year, this interview would never have happened. And one of the things is I created a college circuit for us so we would go to these college — right around the time the concept of the college circuit, which it fortified, among other things, Louis Armstrong and the All-Stars and Dave Brubeck and blah-blah-blah was about to disappear. But I didn’t know that or at least I wasn’t willing to admit it. So I was up at Hamilton in conjunction with a person I knew who was thinking of going to Hamilton. And when I got there I had my trumpet with me because I was still in the Columbia Marching Band. And we were known for being zany and weird. And the Columbia band was really known for doing some outlandish stuff in my day. I mean before I went to school for instance Kennedy showed up, John Kennedy, at the Harvard Columbia game in November of ’63, early November of ’63. And they just re-wrote the entire halftime show on the spot as a political satire and President Silverwater it was, the country will go forward. And then they marched backwards off the field playing some weird song. And

Kennedy loved it. Of course why wouldn’t he, but I mean it wasn’t the playing or the song but the whole riff. And so that’s the band. And we, Columbia University Marching band is known for launching what is now a little bit more known which are these novelty orchestras that get pretty wild and non-musical, that the intellectual colleges do for their halftime shows. And when I got to Hamilton I discovered that they had one too. And it was even a little bit more skiffle than ours. It was the Aaron Burr Lucky Shot Marching and Kazoo Orchestra. And I thought that was funny. I thought it was a great name, great concept and I had my trumpet with me and I said I don’t know any of your music and they said we don’t have any music to show you and I said all right let’s have fun anyway. And I went out there, was Hamilton playing Cortland State? They were playing, I think it was Cortland State, and I went out there and I played with the Aaron Burr Lucky Shot Marching and Kazoo Orchestra. And of course Alexander Hamilton went to Columbia you know. So we have our own feelings about this too.
I see. And what year was this again?
This would have been the fall of 1973.
Okay. We’ll have to tell some people about that at the school.

In between the Charlie Parker Festival and the Fletcher Henderson Festival, I went to Hamilton, New York and played in a football game as a member of the Aaron Burr Lucky Shot Marching and Kazoo Orchestra.
Wow. I wonder if it’s on film, what do you think, Tim? Boy wouldn’t that be something if we had a film of that.
Yeah. I doubt you’d have a film of the halftime show. That’d be great.
We’ll have to look in the archives.
